title: God's Children Love in Action
overview: John tells his readers they are God's children now, and argues that this shows in turning away from wrongdoing and in practical love for one another.

parts.label: Called God's children (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: John marvels that God treats ordinary, flawed people as his own children, even though the wider world does not see it, just as it did not recognize Jesus. Their future is not yet fully clear, but John is sure that when Christ appears they will see him and become like him, and that hope moves them to live cleanly now.

parts.label: Sin and God's family (vv. 4-10)
parts.note: John calls sin a rejection of God's ways and says Jesus came to remove sin and undo the devil's work, so a life of ongoing wrongdoing does not fit God's children. Because John earlier admits believers do sin (1:8), most readers take his stark contrast between God's children and the devil's as being about a settled pattern of life, not a single failure.

parts.label: Love versus Cain (vv. 11-15)
parts.note: Cain, the man in Genesis who killed his brother Abel, is John's picture of the opposite of the love his readers were taught from the start. John says hating a fellow believer is murder at heart, while love shows someone has moved from death into real life.

parts.label: Love that costs something (vv. 16-18)
parts.note: For John, Jesus giving up his life shows what love is, and his followers should be ready to give themselves for each other too. He makes it concrete: if you have plenty and ignore someone in need, your claim to God's love rings hollow.

parts.label: When your heart accuses you (vv. 19-24)
parts.note: Even when our own conscience condemns us, God knows everything and is greater than our hearts; most read this as comfort, though some take it as a sober reminder that God sees all. John sums up God's command as trusting Jesus and loving one another, and says God's Spirit, his presence within believers, assures them he lives in them.

disagreement: Christians differ on what John means when he says those born of God do not sin (vv. 6-9): most take it as describing a settled direction of life rather than perfection, while some traditions hold that real freedom from deliberate sin is possible in this life.
think: Do you think the way a person treats someone in need says more about them than what they say they believe?
